title: Drawing Life Cycle Diagrams
keyIdea: A life cycle diagram shows the stages of a living thing in order, drawn in a circle with arrows, because the young grow up and the cycle begins again. A butterfly goes egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult. A frog goes spawn → tadpole → froglet → adult frog. A flowering plant goes seed → seedling → plant → flower → fruit with seeds. The arrows show the order; the circle shows that offspring start the same pattern again.

kid: A life cycle is the story of how a living thing grows and makes new life. We draw it as a circle with arrows so you can see it goes round and round.
A butterfly starts as an egg. The egg hatches into a caterpillar (the larva). The caterpillar becomes a chrysalis (the pupa). Then an adult butterfly comes out and lays new eggs.
A frog starts as spawn (eggs in jelly). A tadpole hatches. It grows legs and becomes a froglet. The froglet grows into an adult frog, which lays more spawn.
A flowering plant starts as a seed. The seed grows into a seedling, then a plant. The plant makes a flower. The flower makes a fruit with seeds inside, and the cycle can start again.
adult: Year 5 science in England asks children to describe life cycles of a mammal, an amphibian, an insect and a bird. It also covers how some plants and animals reproduce. Year 2 already covers animals having offspring. This lesson is about drawing the cycle as a circle with stages in order and arrows between them.

Draw the stages in order. Draw arrows to show what comes next. Close the loop because offspring start the same stages again. A butterfly and a frog change a lot as they grow. A mammal has a simpler pattern. Plants close the loop with seeds.

Common mistakes: drawing stages in a straight line and forgetting the return arrow; mixing up larva and pupa; putting adult before egg; and thinking a life cycle ends at the adult instead of going on through offspring.
In the lab your child builds a butterfly cycle, a frog cycle and a plant cycle by placing stages on a circle, fixes a broken diagram with a missing arrow, and spots one stage in the wrong place.

familyTip: Find a picture of a frog or a butterfly online or in a book and point to each stage in order. Then draw a big circle on paper, write the four stages around it, and add arrows. Grow cress or beans on wet paper and photograph each stage for a real plant cycle.

visual.caption: Butterfly stage or frog stage? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build butterfly, frog and plant life cycles on a circle, fix a missing arrow, and spot a stage in the wrong place.

practice.prompt: What comes after the caterpillar in a butterfly life cycle?
practice.hint: The caterpillar wraps up before the adult appears.
practice.explain: The larva (caterpillar) becomes a pupa (chrysalis), then the adult butterfly emerges.

practice.prompt: Why do we draw a life cycle as a circle?
choices: because offspring start the same stages again
practice.explain: Adults produce offspring, so the pattern of stages starts again. The circle shows that.
Spawn hatches into tadpoles. Froglets come later, when legs have grown.

practice.prompt: A butterfly cycle has {a} stages. You also draw {b} arrows. How many labels and arrows together?
practice.hint: Count the stage labels and the arrows, then add those two numbers.
practice.explain: {a} stage labels + {b} arrows = {=a+b} marks on the diagram.

practice.prompt: You study {a} animal cycles and {b} plant cycles. How many cycles is that in total?
practice.hint: Add the animal cycles to the plant cycles.

pool.prompt: The larva of a butterfly is called a…
pool.hint: It is the eating, growing stage.
pool.explain: Larva = caterpillar. The chrysalis is the pupa. Spawn is frog eggs.

choices: a young frog with legs, still growing
pool.hint: It looks almost like a small frog.
pool.explain: A froglet has legs and looks like a tiny frog; it grows into an adult.

pool.prompt: What is wrong with egg → adult → pupa → larva?
choices: the stages are in the wrong order
pool.hint: Follow a real butterfly. Keep the stages in order around the circle.
pool.explain: The order should be egg → larva → pupa → adult.

pool.prompt: A life cycle diagram needs arrows because…
choices: they show the order of the stages
pool.hint: Which way does time go?. Keep the stages in order around the circle.
pool.explain: Arrows show which stage comes next around the circle.

pool.prompt: Which is a plant life-cycle stage?
pool.hint: Only one is a plant. Keep the stages in order around the circle.
pool.explain: A seedling is a young plant. Tadpole and chrysalis are animal stages.

pool.prompt: A cycle has {a} stages and you already drew {b} arrows. How many arrows still needed for a full circle?
pool.hint: A full circle needs as many arrows as stages. Subtract the ones you already drew.
pool.explain: {a} stages need {a} arrows. You have {b}, so you still need {=a-b}.

pool.prompt: Mia draws egg → caterpillar → butterfly and stops. What is missing?
choices: the pupa (chrysalis) stage and the return to eggs
pool.hint: Butterfly metamorphosis has four stages, and adults lay eggs.
pool.explain: She skipped the pupa and the arrow back to new eggs that close the cycle.

pool.prompt: Why is adult → egg a valid arrow on a life cycle?
choices: adults produce the next generation of eggs
eggs grow into adults directly in one step
pool.explain: Reproduction links adult back to egg (or seed or live young), which is why the diagram is a loop.

pool.prompt: You draw {a} butterfly stages and {b} frog stages. How many stage labels is that?
pool.hint: Add the butterfly labels to the frog labels.
